note: RECONSTRUCTION of Allport & Ross (1967) pp. 433-434 from secondary sources; the paper is closed access and was not read. Each sentence is quoted as a later source quotes it. Every page-citing source places both paragraphs on p. 434. 'wording' on a quoted_by entry records how that source's wording differs from the sentence text; entries without it quote the sentence verbatim.
method: Built on the fragments in drafts_b.json (Bulbulia 2013, Wikipedia, Flere et al., Neyrinck et al. 2010, Tønnesvang 2003). New sources found by exact-phrase web search, PMC/Europe PMC full-text search with E-utilities efetch for the XML, Bing results pages, DOAJ API, and PDFs downloaded to the session scratchpad and read with pypdf. The hypothesised sentences from the brief were confirmed one by one; the two not in the brief (the axiology sentence; 'In theological terms ...') were found quoted in McKenna, Francis & Stewart (2025).

extrinsic.reconstructed_text: Persons with this orientation are disposed to use religion for their own ends. The term is borrowed from axiology, to designate an interest that is held because it serves other, more ultimate interests. Extrinsic values are always instrumental and utilitarian. Persons with this orientation may find religion useful in a variety of ways—to provide security and solace, sociability and distraction, status and self-justification. The embraced creed is lightly held or else selectively shaped to fit more primary needs. In theological terms the extrinsic type turns to God, but without turning away from self.

intrinsic.reconstructed_text: Persons with this orientation find their master motive in religion. Other needs, strong as they may be, are regarded as of less ultimate significance, and they are, so far as possible, brought into harmony with the religious beliefs and prescriptions. Having embraced a creed the individual endeavors to internalize it and follow it fully. It is in this sense that he lives his religion.

summary_sentence.agreement: 5 sources cite the sentence to Allport & Ross 1967 (three to p. 434) but in three wordings: 'person ... person ... lives his religion' (Sakellariou 2025; Kayıklık 2015), 'individual ... lives his' (Flere et al.), 'uses his religion, the intrinsically motivated lives his' (Pincus 2022), plural paraphrase (Zheng et al. 2020). The two-source wording is given as text; 'individual' versus 'person' and whether 'religion' is repeated after 'lives his' remain open. The sentence is separate from the two definitional paragraphs: McKenna 2025 (which block-quotes both) does not include it in them, and the Wikipedia article does not contain it despite search-engine summaries saying so.
